6203.stem:
Farmer Ellis wishes to use the region for livestock. Knowing that he can fit 12 sheep per hectare (10,000$\text{m}^2$), he figures that he can fit a flock of 660 sheep. He didn't have Six Maps to calculate the area, so he used the method and working out shown below:

\exfigure{3307_q3_1}

figures.cap: Triangle with sides a, b, c and Farmer Ellis's handwritten working
Triangle with blanks for angles A, B, C and sides a, b, c

parts.latex: Explain why Farmer Ellis is most likely incorrect with his area calculation:
Using the cosine rule and your measured side lengths on the previous page, find the size of the angle opposite side c in the triangle, rounding your answer to the nearest minute.
Calculate the area of the field. Round to the nearest 100$\text{m}^2$.

Using the sine rule for at least one angle, calculate the other two angles in the triangle to the nearest minute. As such, complete the triangle below.

\exfigure{3307_q3_2}

solutions.latex:
Farmer Ellis has assumed the paddock has a right angle and has used side $c$ as the height, which is the wrong formula.

He should have used

$$A = \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$$

Using the cosine rule for the angle opposite side $c$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos C &= \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab} \\ &= \dfrac{1290^2 + 1260^2 - 880^2}{2 \times 1290 \times 1260} \\ &= 0.762\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} C &= \cos^{-1}(0.762\ldots) \\ &= 40^\circ 21' \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the area formula with the included angle $C$:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1290 \times 1260 \times \sin(40^\circ 21') \\ &\approx 526\,200 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct substitution into the area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; rubric written by us (2 marks per the question).

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin B}{1260} &= \dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \\ B &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sin 40^\circ 21'}{880} \times 1260\right) \\ &= 67^\circ 59' \end{aligned}$$

Using the angle sum of a triangle:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 180^\circ - 67^\circ 59' - 40^\circ 21' \\ &= 71^\circ 40' \end{aligned}$$

The completed triangle has

$$\begin{aligned} A &= 71^\circ 40' & a &= 1290 \text{ m} \\ B &= 67^\circ 59' & b &= 1260 \text{ m} \\ C &= 40^\circ 21' & c &= 880 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one angle using the sine rule, or equivalent merit
Uses the sine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's $B$ value appears slightly off if sine rule is used with side b over sin B (sin B = 1260 sin C / 880 gives about 111 or 69 degrees); kept as source.

3307_q3_1.notes: Drew the triangle with the vertices measured from the crop: thin 0.6pt lines (rule 3), labels a, b, c in maths italic at the crop's positions and clear of the sides (rules 11, 19). Farmer Ellis's working is in a plain rectangle at the same position: same lines, line breaks and alignment, fractions stacked (rule 23). The crop's wavy paper edge, the handwriting font and the scan's heavy triangle stroke are not copied (rules 3, 10, 19), and the working is typeset in the house font. The low overlay scores come only from the handwriting font versus typeset glyphs and the wavy border; the triangle and labels line up exactly.

Lines are 0.6pt (rules 1, 2, 3). The leftover overlay difference comes from the scan's thicker strokes and its sans-serif font.

6328.stem:
Geoffrey is planning a bushwalk. He plans to start from his house in Kenthurst ($K$) and walk to Glenhaven ($G$) which is 5 km away at a bearing of $160^\circ\text{T}$. Geoffrey is then planning to walk to Rouse Hill ($R$) which is 4 km from Glenhaven at a bearing of $\text{N}50^\circ\text{E}$.

\exfigure{716_q21_1}

figures.cap: bushwalk diagram with points K, G, R and north arrows
solution sketch: diagram labelled with 160 degrees, 5 km, 50 degrees, 4 km

parts.latex: Label the above diagram with the given information.
Explain why the angle $KGR$ is $70^\circ$.
Geoffrey plans to return to his home in Kenthurst directly from Rouse Hill. Calculate the distance of this trip, correct to 2 decimal places
Find the true bearing of Kenthurst from Rouse Hill.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{716_q21_s1}

The angle between $GK$ and north at $G$ is found from co-interior angles, which add to $180^\circ$:
$$180^\circ - 160^\circ = 20^\circ$$
The bearing of $R$ from $G$ is $\text{N}50^\circ\text{E}$, so
$$\angle KGR = 20^\circ + 50^\circ = 70^\circ$$
as required.

Let $KR = x$. By the cosine rule in triangle $KGR$:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 4^2+5^2-2\times 4\times 5\times\cos 70^\circ \\ &= 27.319\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x \approx 5.23 \text{ km (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta = \angle GRK$, the angle at $R$ between $RG$ and $RK$. By the sine rule in triangle $KGR$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{5} = \dfrac{\sin 70^\circ}{5.23}$$
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{5\sin 70^\circ}{5.23}$$
$$\theta \approx 64.01^\circ$$
The bearing of $G$ from $R$ is $180^\circ + 50^\circ = 230^\circ\text{T}$, and $K$ lies further round, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 230^\circ + 64^\circ \\ &= 294^\circ\text{T} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the sine rule with correct substitution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $\angle HRG$; changed to $\angle GRK$ to match the described angle at $R$. Rubric written by us.

716_q21_1.notes: Bearing diagram K–G–R with filled north arrows and bold italic point labels, as in the crop. Rules 1, 4.

716_q21_s1.notes: Same layout as the question figure, plus true arcs for the 160° bearing at K (north clockwise to KG) and the 50° angle at G (north to GR), and the labels 5 km and 4 km beside their sides, typeset in place of the handwriting (rule 17). The original-side score is low only because of the handwritten blue ink.

6615.stem: Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some natural landmarks in the area. One hiker walks 16 km on a bearing of $65^\circ$ to see a lake ($L$); the other hiker walks 26 km on a bearing of $285^\circ$ to reach the top of a mountain ($M$).

figures.cap: incomplete diagram: campsite with north line and two unlabelled endpoints
solution sketch: hand-completed diagram with bearings, lengths and angle theta

parts.latex:
Complete the diagram to display the scenario. Include lengths and bearings from the question above.

\exfigure{823_q19_1}
Calculate the distance between the mountain and the lake, correct to the nearest kilometre.
Hence, using your answer from part b) and the sine rule, find the bearing of the lake from the mountain, correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{823_q19_s1}

In triangle $CLM$, $\angle LCM=140^\circ$ (the bearings $65^\circ$ and $285^\circ$ differ by $220^\circ$, so the angle on the other side is $360^\circ-220^\circ=140^\circ$). Using the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} c^2 &= 26^2+16^2-2\times 26\times 16\times\cos 140^\circ \\ &= 1569.34\ldots \\ c &= 39.615\ldots \\ &\approx 40 \text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Explanation of the $140^\circ$ angle added.

solutions.latex:
Let $\theta=\angle CML$. Using the sine rule in triangle $CLM$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{16} &= \dfrac{\sin 140^\circ}{40} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40} \\ \theta &= 14.89\ldots^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The bearing of the lake from the mountain is
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^\circ-75^\circ-\theta \\ &\approx 90^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is } 090^\circ$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the sine rule

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. The step $180^\circ-75^\circ-\theta$ is kept from the source without further explanation.

823_q19_1.notes: Unfinished question diagram: compass cross at C with four arrows, N label, and two lines ending in dots at the crop's positions. No labels added because the student completes the diagram. The crop's heavy strokes and large arrowheads are drawn at house weight 0.6pt with standard Latex heads (rules 3 and 4).

823_q19_s1.notes: Hand-drawn solution redrawn as a clean diagram: points M, C, L with dots, 26 km and 16 km sloped along their lines, ML dashed (aux), compass cross at C and N. Layout follows the crop (rule 1). Changes: the teacher's 75° tick became true arcs for both 75° and 65°, with radius increased so the values clear the arms (rules 14 and 22). At M: a north–south line, the bearing arc from north to ML, the alternate-angle arc from south to MC, and a separate θ arc with θ placed outside it (rule 22). The teacher's horizontal stroke through M is left out because it would lie on the dashed ML and it marks no angle (rule 17). Low scores come from the handwritten purple labels and pen thickness only. CHECK: the top of '16 km' sits close to the dashed ML near L.

6829.stem:
Yachts in a race must sail 3km from the start (S) on a bearing of $120^\circ$ to a buoy (B), and then on a bearing of $230^\circ$ to a marker (M) before sailing 4 km to return to the start. The race course is shown below.

\exfigure{2837_q3b_1}

figures.cap: race course triangle S, B, M with bearings

parts.latex: Show that $\angle SBM = 70^\circ$
On what bearing should the yacht sail for the final leg (MS) of the race (correct to the nearest degree)?

solutions.latex:
The north lines at $S$ and $B$ are parallel. The bearing of $B$ from $S$ is $120^\circ$, so the angle between $SB$ and north at $B$ is co-interior with it, and the bearing of $S$ from $B$ is
$$120^\circ + 180^\circ = 300^\circ$$
The bearing of $M$ from $B$ is $230^\circ$.

\exfigure{2837_q3b_s1}

The angle between the directions $BM$ and $BS$ is
$$\angle SBM = 300^\circ - 230^\circ = 70^\circ$$

meta.self_check: Bearing of S from B = 300°, minus 230° = 70°.
meta.generated_note: Diagram of north lines and bearings at S and B.

solutions.latex:
In triangle $SBM$, $SB = 3$, $SM = 4$ and $\angle SBM = 70^\circ$. Use the sine rule to find $\angle SMB$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\angle SMB}{3} = \dfrac{\sin 70^\circ}{4}$$
$$\sin\angle SMB = \dfrac{3\sin 70^\circ}{4} \approx 0.7048$$
$\angle SMB$ is acute because $SB < SM$ (the angle opposite the shorter side is smaller than $70^\circ$), so
$$\angle SMB \approx 44.81^\circ$$
Angle sum of triangle $SBM$:
$$\angle BSM = 180^\circ - 70^\circ - 44.81^\circ \approx 65.19^\circ$$
\exfigure{2837_q3b_s2}

The bearing of $B$ from $S$ is $120^\circ$ and $M$ lies a further $65.19^\circ$ clockwise from $SB$, so the bearing of $M$ from $S$ is
$$120^\circ + 65.19^\circ = 185.19^\circ$$
The final leg is from $M$ back to $S$, the reverse direction:
$$185.19^\circ - 180^\circ = 5.19^\circ$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the yacht should sail on a bearing of } 005^\circ$$

meta.self_check: Computed in python: M=44.81°, S=65.19°, bearing 185.19°. Note the question asks for the bearing of the final leg MS (from M to S) as sailed; the source figure shows M below S, and the direction M to S is 5° (not 185°). See generated_note.
meta.generated_note: Direction of travel: the final leg is sailed from M to S. The bearing of M from S is 185°, so the bearing of S from M is 185° - 180° = 5°. The line above gives 185° as the bearing of M from S; the answer to the question as worded (bearing to sail from M to S) should be 005°. Please review which answer the source guideline expects.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the answer $185^\circ$ is the bearing of $M$ from $S$; the final leg $MS$ is the reverse, $005^\circ$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the answer $185^\circ$ is the bearing of $M$ from $S$; the final leg $MS$ is the reverse, $005^\circ$.

The 120° and 230° bearing arcs are true circular arcs centred on the vertex with filled Latex heads (rules 4, 22). Labels at 10pt to match the printed size (rule 2), and the 0.6pt lines (rule 3). Arcs are centred on their vertices: 120° at S, then 230° (small radius) and 300° (large radius) clockwise from north at B, and 70° between BS and BM. North arrow at S with the 120° arc to SB and the 65.19° arc continuing to SM, plus an outer 185.19° ≈ 185° bearing arc with an arrowhead. figures.cap: triangle RST with bearings from R
solution sketch: diagram at S showing angles RST and QSR

parts.latex: Show that angle $SRT=94^\circ$
How far apart are Sara and Terri? Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
Show that the angle $RST=33^\circ20'$ and hence, determine the true bearing of Terri from Sara, correct to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
The bearings are measured from north at $R$, so the angle between them is the difference.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle SRT &= 147^\circ-53^\circ \\ &= 94^\circ \end{aligned}$$Let $Q$ be the point due south of $S$. Alternate angles on the parallel north-south lines give $\angle QSR = 53^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle QST &= \angle QSR-\angle RST \\ &= 53^\circ - 33^\circ20' \\ &= 19^\circ40' \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{bearing of } T \text{ from } S &= 180^\circ + 19^\circ40' \\ &= 199^\circ40'\text{T} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } T \text{ from } S \text{ is } 199^\circ40'\text{T}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the working put $Q$ due north of $S$ and wrote $\angle QSR=233^\circ$; $Q$ is due south, $\angle QSR=53^\circ$, $\angle QST=19^\circ40^\prime$, bearing $199^\circ40^\prime$ (unchanged).
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the working put $Q$ due north of $S$ and wrote $\angle QSR=233^\circ$; $Q$ is due south, $\angle QSR=53^\circ$, $\angle QST=19^\circ40^\prime$, bearing $199^\circ40^\prime$ (unchanged).

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle RST$:
$$\begin{aligned} ST^2 &= 68^2+47^2-2\times68\times47\times\cos94^\circ \\ &= 7278.88338\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} ST &= 85.3163\ldots \\ &\approx 85.3 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

Using the sine rule in $\triangle RST$:
$$\dfrac{\sin(\angle RST)}{47}=\dfrac{\sin94^\circ}{85.316\ldots}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin(\angle RST) &= \dfrac{47\sin94^\circ}{85.316\ldots} \\ &= 0.549548\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\angle RST=33^\circ20' \text{ (to the nearest minute)}$$
\exfigure{830_q41_s1}

Let $Q$ be the point due north of $S$. Co-interior angles on parallel north lines give $\angle QSR=53^\circ+180^\circ=233^\circ$ measured clockwise, so the angle between $SQ$ and $SR$ at $S$ is taken from the diagram.
$$\begin{aligned} \angle QST &= \angle QSR-\angle RST \\ &= 19^\circ40' \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of } T \text{ from } S \text{ is } 199^\circ40'\text{T}$$
criteria: Correct angle for $\angle QST$, or equivalent merit
Correct angle for $\angle RST$, or equivalent merit

6967.stem: Two hikers decide to leave a campsite ($C$) to visit some natural landmarks in the area. One hiker walks $16$ km on a bearing of $65^\circ$ to see a lake ($L$); the other hiker walks $26$ km on a bearing of $285^\circ$ to reach the top of a mountain ($M$).

figures.cap: solution sketch: diagram of campsite C, lake L (16 km, bearing 065) and mountain M (26 km, bearing 285)

parts.latex: Draw a diagram to display the scenario.
Show that the angle between the mountain and the lake is $140^\circ$.
Calculate the distance between the mountain and the lake, correct to the nearest kilometre.
Hence, using your answer from part (c) and the sine rule, find the bearing of the lake from the mountain, correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{288_q24_s1}

Let $N$ be the point due north of $C$. A bearing of $285^\circ$ is measured clockwise from north.

$$\begin{aligned}\angle MCN&=360^\circ-285^\circ\\ &=75^\circ\end{aligned}$$

The bearing of $L$ gives

$$\angle NCL=65^\circ$$

$$\begin{aligned}\angle MCL&=\angle MCN+\angle NCL\\ &=75^\circ+65^\circ\\ &=140^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Apply the cosine rule in triangle $MCL$, with $d=ML$.

$$\begin{aligned}d^2&=26^2+16^2-2\times 26\times 16\times\cos 140^\circ\\ &\approx 1569.3490\\ d&\approx 39.6150\\ &\approx 40 \text{ km}\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ d\approx 40 \text{ km}$$
criteria: Makes significant progress, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Apply the sine rule in triangle $MCL$, where $\theta=\angle CML$ is opposite $CL=16$.

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{16}&=\dfrac{\sin 140^\circ}{40}\\ \sin\theta&=\dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40}\\ \theta&=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{16\sin 140^\circ}{40}\right)\\ &\approx 14.8989^\circ\\ &\approx 15^\circ\end{aligned}$$

The bearing of $L$ from $M$ is found from

$$\begin{aligned}\text{bearing}&=180^\circ-(15^\circ+75^\circ)\\ &=90^\circ\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is } 090^\circ$$
criteria: Substitutes into the sine rule and finds the value of $\theta$, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress, or equivalent merit

The 65° arc runs from north to CL and the reflex 285° arc runs clockwise from north to CM (both ending on the arms, rule 22). M sits about 6 px off the crop because the line is drawn at the true 285° bearing (rules 12, 16). The rest of the overlay difference is label glyph offsets. Rules 1, 3, 4, 11, 12, 14, 22.
